short_def: The distance between two holes. VEX IQ sizes are counted in pitch.
explanation: 1 pitch = 12.7 mm (half an inch). Shafts, standoffs and rope are named by length in pitch: a 4x pitch shaft is 4 pitches long.
example: We need a 4x pitch standoff to fill this gap.

short_def: How beams and plates are named: holes across x holes long.
explanation: A 1x8 beam is 1 hole wide and 8 holes long. A 4x4 plate is 4 holes by 4 holes. Count the holes to find a part's size.
example: Can you pass me a 2x8 beam?

short_def: Shifted to the side, so holes don't line up with the usual grid.
explanation: Offset parts (e.g. offset corner connectors) shift the attachment point, which helps when parts don't quite line up.
example: Use an offset connector so the gear meshes.

short_def: How far a wheel rolls in one full turn.
explanation: Tires are labeled by travel, e.g. 200mm travel. VEXcode needs the wheel travel to drive exact distances.
example: Our wheels have 200 mm travel.

short_def: The number of teeth on a gear or sprocket, written like 36T.
explanation: Gears and sprockets are named by tooth count. Comparing tooth counts tells you the gear ratio.
example: Swap the 12T gear for a 36T gear.

short_def: The robot's computer. Motors and sensors plug into it.
explanation: Runs your program, has a screen and buttons, and 12 Smart Ports. In VEXcode it is called the Brain.
example: Plug the motor into port 3 on the Brain.

short_def: Handheld device the driver uses to control the robot.
explanation: Has two joysticks and several buttons. It connects to the Brain wirelessly or with a tether cable.
example: Pair the controller with the Brain before the match.

short_def: Rechargeable battery that powers the Brain and motors.
explanation: Charge it before every practice and competition. A low battery makes motors weak and slow.
example: Is the battery charged?

short_def: Motor that spins a shaft and can measure how far it turned.
explanation: It has a built-in sensor (encoder), so code can turn it an exact number of degrees or turns.
example: This arm needs a second Smart Motor.

short_def: A numbered socket on the Brain where motors and sensors plug in.
explanation: The Brain has 12 Smart Ports. Any device can go in any port, but your code must use the right port number.
example: The left motor is in port 1.

short_def: Cable that connects a motor or sensor to a Smart Port.
explanation: Comes in lengths from 200 mm to 600 mm in the kit. Use the shortest one that reaches.
example: This cable is too short; get a 400 mm one.

short_def: Cable that connects the Brain or controller to a computer.
explanation: Used to download programs, update firmware and charge.
example: Plug the USB cable into the Brain to download.

short_def: Sensor you can tap, which can also light up in different colors.
explanation: Code can detect a press and set its color, e.g. green when the robot is ready.
example: Tap the Touch LED to start the program.

short_def: Sensor that detects when it is pressed or bumped.
explanation: Often used to detect a wall or to stop an arm at its limit.
example: Put a bumper switch where the arm stops.

short_def: Sensor that detects color, brightness and nearby objects.
explanation: Measures hue (color) and brightness, and can tell when an object is very close.
example: The Optical Sensor checks the color of the game piece.

short_def: Sensor that measures how far away an object is.
explanation: Can measure distance to a wall or object, and is used to stop the robot at the right place.
example: Drive until the Distance Sensor reads 100 mm.

short_def: Tool for pushing in and pulling out pins and other parts.
explanation: It has three ends: a pusher, a puller and a lever. Use it instead of fingernails or teeth!
example: Use the pin tool to pull out that pin.

short_def: Stretchy band that stores energy or pulls parts together.
explanation: Used in intakes, catapults and to hold mechanisms in place. The kit has silicone rubber bands.
example: Add a rubber band to make the claw grip harder.

short_def: Part that gives a rubber band a place to hook on.
explanation: Attach it to the robot, then loop the rubber band around it.
example: Hook the band onto the rubber band anchor.

short_def: Clip that holds a Smart Cable in place on the robot.
explanation: Keeps cables tidy so they don't get caught in moving parts.
example: Use cable anchors so the cable doesn't hit the gears.

short_def: Rope with loops on the ends, used with a spool to pull things.
explanation: Named by length in pitch, e.g. 24x pitch rope.
example: The rope pulls the lift up.

short_def: Part that winds up rope when it turns.
explanation: A spool on a motor shaft with rope makes a winch, which can pull a lift up.
example: The spool winds the rope.

short_def: Flexible flap that attaches to chain to grab game pieces.
explanation: Comes in short, medium and large. Attach flaps to chain or tread to build an intake.
example: Add more intake flaps so it grabs the ball.

short_def: Grippy link that attaches to chain or tread.
explanation: Adds grip to chain or tread, for example in an intake.
example: Traction links help the intake grip the cube.

short_def: Belt of links that wraps around sprockets, like on a tank.
explanation: Built from tank tread links. Used for treaded drivetrains or intakes.
example: Tank tread can climb over small bumps.

short_def: A gear and a catch that let something turn only one way.
explanation: The pawl drops into the ratchet's teeth so it can't turn backward.
example: The ratchet stops the lift from falling down.

short_def: Spring part that pushes back when it is squeezed.
explanation: Comes in weak and strong versions. Absorbs bumps or stores energy.
example: Use a strong shock absorber for the bumper.

short_def: Heavy wheel that stores spinning energy.
explanation: Keeps spinning steadily, which helps launchers shoot consistently.
example: The flywheel launches the ball.

short_def: Thin, bendable plastic sheet with holes.
explanation: Used for ramps, guides and walls. Attach it with sheet pins.
example: Make a ramp out of a plastic sheet.

short_def: Pin that holds a thin sheet onto the robot.
explanation: Made for plastic sheets, paper or card.
example: Use sheet pins to attach the plastic sheet.

short_def: Rubber belt with ridges that grabs and pulls in game pieces.
explanation: Comes in small and large sizes.
example: The intake belt pulls the ball into the robot.

short_def: Square metal rod that carries turning motion.
explanation: It is square so wheels and gears turn with it. Named by length in pitch, e.g. 4x pitch shaft.
example: Slide the gear onto the shaft.

short_def: Shaft made to fit into a Smart Motor.
explanation: Comes in metal and plastic, named by length in pitch.
example: Put a motor shaft in the motor first.

short_def: Shaft with a cap on one end so it can't slide out.
explanation: The cap holds parts on, so you need fewer shaft collars.
example: A capped shaft holds the wheel on.

short_def: Shaft made of plastic: lighter, but it bends more easily.
explanation: Good for parts that don't carry much load.
example: Use a metal shaft here; the plastic one bends.

short_def: Rubber ring that grips a shaft so parts don't slide off.
explanation: Push it onto the end of a shaft to hold wheels and gears in place.
example: Add a shaft collar so the wheel doesn't fall off.

short_def: Small ring on a shaft that fills the gap between parts.
explanation: Keeps gears and wheels in the right position along a shaft.
example: Add a spacer so the gear lines up.

short_def: Thin, flat ring that reduces rubbing between parts.
explanation: Put it between a spinning part and the structure so it turns smoothly.
example: Put a washer between the wheel and the beam.

short_def: Part that joins beams and plates at a right angle.
explanation: Named by width (1x or 2x wide), size (1x2, 2x2…) and number of sides (double, triple). In Chinese, 1x/2x wide = 单脚/双脚, and double/triple = 双头/三头.
example: Use a corner connector to attach the wall to the base.

short_def: Strong corner connector used to build a chassis frame.
explanation: Comes in large and small, and left and right versions.
example: Use chassis corner connectors on the drivetrain.

short_def: Small plastic pin that snaps two parts together.
explanation: Named by length on each side: 1x1, 1x2, 2x2. The kit has more of these than anything else.
example: Use 1x1 pins to join the two beams.

short_def: Pin with a cap on one side, so it only sticks out one way.
explanation: Named like 0x2: 0 on the capped side, 2 on the other side.
example: Use a capped pin so it doesn't stick out.

short_def: Pin with a round end so a gear can spin freely on it.
explanation: Gears on idler pins are not driven by a shaft; they just pass motion along.
example: Put the middle gear on an idler pin.

short_def: Post that holds two parts apart at a set distance.
explanation: Named by length in pitch. Join them to beams and plates with standoff connectors.
example: Use 2x pitch standoffs to make the frame wider.

short_def: Part that joins a standoff to beams, plates or other standoffs.
explanation: Types include mini, end, 90°, 45°, straight and truss.
example: Use an end standoff connector here.

short_def: Round part that rolls; made of a hub and a tire.
explanation: Choose wheels by size (travel) and grip.
example: Our robot has four wheels.

short_def: The center of a wheel, which fits onto a shaft.
explanation: A tire stretches over the hub.
example: Put the tire onto the hub.

short_def: The rubber outside part of a wheel that grips the floor.
explanation: Different tires give different grip and travel.
example: This tire grips the field tiles well.

short_def: Wheel with small rollers, so it can also slide sideways.
explanation: Omni wheels let a drivetrain turn smoothly.
example: Omni wheels help our robot turn.

short_def: Soft, puffy tire with extra grip and bounce.
explanation: Named by diameter in pitch, e.g. 5x pitch diameter balloon tire.
example: Balloon tires give the robot more grip.

short_def: Long, narrow structural piece with a row of holes.
explanation: Named by holes: a 1x8 beam is 1 hole wide and 8 holes long. 2x beams are 2 holes wide.
example: Use two 1x12 beams for the arm.

short_def: Flat, wide structural piece with a grid of holes.
explanation: Named by holes, e.g. 4x8 plate. VEX China calls plates 矩形块.
example: Build the base from a 4x8 plate.

short_def: Beam bent at an angle, such as 30°, 45° or 60°.
explanation: Named by size and angle, e.g. 3x3 60° angle beam.
example: Use a 45° angle beam to make the ramp.

short_def: L-shaped beam with a 90° corner.
explanation: Named by size, e.g. 3x5 right angle beam.
example: A right angle beam makes the corner.

short_def: T-shaped beam.
explanation: Joins three directions in one part.
example: Use a tee beam where the arms meet.

short_def: Beam with a square hole that locks onto a shaft, so both turn together.
explanation: Types include center lock, end lock and round lock beams. Used to attach arms to a shaft.
example: Lock the arm to the shaft with a lock beam.

short_def: Beam with a bend, used to build corners. Has left and right versions.
explanation: Comes in sizes like 1x1, 2x1 and 2x2, plus extended versions.
example: Use a left corner beam on this side.

short_def: Wheel with teeth that meshes with another gear to pass on turning.
explanation: Named by tooth count: 12T, 24T, 36T, 48T, 60T. Meshing gears turn in opposite directions.
example: The 12T gear drives the 60T gear.

short_def: Screw-shaped gear that turns a normal gear slowly and strongly.
explanation: A worm gear can't be turned backward by the gear it drives, so it holds its position.
example: The worm gear holds the arm up.

short_def: Straight strip of gear teeth.
explanation: A gear turning against a rack moves it in a straight line.
example: The rack gear pushes the tray forward.

short_def: Toothed wheel that drives a chain.
explanation: Named by tooth count: 8T, 16T, 24T. Sprockets joined by chain turn the same direction.
example: Put a 16T sprocket on each shaft.

short_def: Loop of links that connects sprockets so they turn together.
explanation: Built by snapping chain links together. Make it tight, but not too tight.
example: The chain came off the sprocket.

short_def: Uneven wheel that pushes something up and down as it turns.
explanation: The kit has large and small drop cams.
example: The cam lifts the lever every turn.

short_def: Part that rides on a cam and moves as the cam turns.
example: The cam follower moves up and down.

short_def: Track that lets a bracket slide along it in a straight line.
explanation: Used with linear motion brackets to build sliders.
example: The tray slides along a linear motion beam.

short_def: Part that slides along a linear motion beam.
explanation: Comes in 1x and 2x pitch versions.
example: Attach the claw to the linear motion bracket.

short_def: Using compressed air to move parts.
explanation: The VEX IQ pneumatics kit includes a pump, air tank, valve, cylinder and tubing.
example: We could use pneumatics for the claw.

short_def: Part that pushes out or pulls in when air goes in.
explanation: Extends and retracts quickly. Controlled by a valve.
example: The cylinder pushes the game piece off.

short_def: Pump that fills the pneumatic system with compressed air.
explanation: Plugs into a Smart Port and is turned on by code.
example: Turn the pump on at the start of the match.

short_def: Container that stores compressed air.
explanation: More stored air means more cylinder movements.
example: Check that the air tank is full.

short_def: Valve controlled by code that sends air to a cylinder.
explanation: Opens or closes to make a cylinder extend or retract.
example: The valve controls both cylinders.

short_def: Plastic tube that carries air between pneumatic parts.
explanation: Cut it to length, and join pieces with fittings.
example: The tubing is leaking; replace it.

short_def: Connector that joins pieces of air tubing.
explanation: T-fittings split air to two places; straight fittings join two tubes.
example: Use a T-fitting to connect two cylinders.

short_def: Plastic cap that snaps onto a Smart Motor to add mounting holes.
explanation: A single mount gives the back of the motor a second set of holes. A double mount joins two motors back to back. Students often call it a motor collar.
example: Use a double motor mount to put the two motors back to back.

aka: continuous linear motion rack gear; rack
short_def: Beam with gear teeth that slides in linear motion brackets.
explanation: A gear turning against the rack makes it slide in a straight line. Continuous racks can be joined end to end to make a longer track. Named by size, e.g. 1x6.
example: The linear motion rack moves the claw forward and back.

short_def: Sensor inside the Brain that measures turning, tilt and acceleration.
explanation: You can't see it, but every Brain has one built in. It contains a gyro, which measures turning (heading and rotation), and an accelerometer, which measures changes in speed. Code uses it for exact turns like "turn to heading 90°". Keep the robot still while it calibrates at the start.
example: Use the inertial sensor so the robot turns exactly 90 degrees.

short_def: Camera sensor that recognizes colors, AprilTags and game objects.
explanation: It finds objects in its camera picture and tells the Brain where they are, so the robot can turn toward or pick up the right game piece. Set up what it looks for in VEXcode's Devices menu.
example: The AI Vision Sensor finds the closest ball and the robot turns to it.

short_def: The app we use to write programs for the VEX IQ robot.
explanation: It has Blocks, Python and C++. It runs on computers and tablets, or in a web browser.
example: Open VEXcode IQ and start a new Blocks project.

short_def: A set of instructions, saved together, that the robot can run.
explanation: VEXcode calls a program a project. Save it, download it to the Brain, then run it.
example: Save the project before you close VEXcode.
blocks:
when started
drive [forward v] for (300) [mm v] ▶
turn [right v] for (90) degrees ▶
set [Pneumatic1 v] [cylinder1 v] to [extend v]

short_def: Send a project from the computer to the robot's Brain.
explanation: Download again after every change, or the robot will run the old version.
example: Did you download the new version?

short_def: Start a project on the robot.
explanation: Press Run in VEXcode, or choose the project on the Brain and press the check button.
example: Run the project and watch what the robot does.

short_def: A piece of code you drag and snap together in VEXcode Blocks.
explanation: Each block does one job. Its shape shows where it can fit.
example: Drag a drive block into the project.

short_def: Block that does an action; it snaps above and below other blocks.
explanation: Most blocks are stack blocks, like drive for and wait.
example: Add a stack block under when started.

short_def: Block with a round top that starts a stack when something happens.
explanation: Nothing can snap above it. when started is a hat block.
example: Every stack needs a hat block on top.

short_def: Block shaped like a C that wraps around other blocks.
explanation: Loops and if blocks are C blocks. They control when the blocks inside run.
example: Put the drive blocks inside the repeat C block.

short_def: Pointed block that reports True or False.
explanation: It fits in the pointed spaces of blocks like if and wait until.
example: Put a Boolean block in the if.

short_def: Round block that reports a value, like a number or text.
explanation: It fits in round spaces in other blocks.
example: Use a reporter block to print the heading.

short_def: Where you tell VEXcode which device is plugged into which port.
explanation: A device's blocks only appear after you add it here.
example: Add the Distance Sensor in the Devices menu, on port 4.

short_def: A note in the code for people to read; the robot ignores it.
explanation: Use comments to explain what each part of the project does.
example: Add a comment that says what this stack does.

short_def: The drive motors, set up in VEXcode to move the robot as one.
explanation: This is the device you configure in code, not the wheels and motors themselves. Its blocks drive and turn the whole robot.
example: Configure a 2-motor drivetrain that uses the inertial sensor.

short_def: Move the robot forward or in reverse until told to stop.
explanation: drive keeps going until another block stops it. drive for goes a set distance.
example: Drive forward until the bumper is pressed.

short_def: Drive a set distance, then stop.
explanation: Choose the direction, distance and unit (mm or inches).
example: Drive forward for 300 mm.

short_def: Turn left or right by a number of degrees from where the robot is now.
explanation: Small errors add up after many turns. turn to heading avoids that.
example: Turn right for 90 degrees.

short_def: Turn to face a direction on the field, from 0 to 359 degrees.
explanation: Uses the Inertial Sensor. Heading is measured from where the robot faced when it calibrated, so errors don't add up.
example: Turn to heading 180 to face the wall.

short_def: Stop the drivetrain.
explanation: How it stops depends on the stopping mode: brake, coast or hold.
example: Stop driving when the bumper is pressed.

short_def: The direction the robot is facing, from 0 to 359.99 degrees.
explanation: After 359 it goes back to 0. VEXcode's Chinese calls it 归位角度; 航向 is also common.
example: Our heading is 90, so we are facing right.

short_def: How far the robot has turned in total, counting every full turn.
explanation: Unlike heading, it doesn't go back to 0: two full turns right is 720. Left turns are negative.
example: After two spins, rotation is 720.

short_def: How fast the robot or a motor moves, as a percent or in rpm.
explanation: Set it before moving. For motors, VEXcode's Chinese uses 转速.
example: Set the drive velocity to 50% for more accuracy.

short_def: Backward. VEXcode says reverse instead of backward.
explanation: Directions in VEXcode are forward and reverse for driving, left and right for turning.
example: Drive in reverse for 100 mm.

short_def: How a motor or drivetrain stops: brake, coast or hold.
explanation: Choose it with set drive stopping or set motor stopping.
example: Set the arm's stopping mode to hold.

short_def: Stopping mode that stops quickly.
explanation: The default for most movements.
example: Brake so the robot stops at the line.

short_def: Stopping mode that lets the motors slow down by themselves.
explanation: Smoother, but the robot rolls a little further.
example: Use coast so the launcher spins down gently.

short_def: Stopping mode that stops and pushes back to stay in place.
explanation: Best for arms and lifts, so they don't fall.
example: Set the lift to hold so it stays up.

short_def: Time limit for a movement; after it, the project moves on.
explanation: Stops the robot getting stuck if it hits something before it finishes.
example: Set a 2-second timeout in case the robot hits the wall.

short_def: Option that lets the next block start before this movement finishes.
explanation: Click the ▶ at the end of a block. Lets the robot move and do something else at the same time.
example: Drive and don't wait, so the arm can lift while driving.
blocks: drive [forward v] for (200) [mm v] ◀ and don't wait

short_def: Reports True when the drivetrain has finished moving.
explanation: Useful with and don't wait, to check when a movement ends.
example: Wait until drive is done, then lower the arm.

short_def: Unit for angles. One full turn is 360 degrees.
explanation: Used for turning the robot, headings and motor positions.
example: Turn right for 90 degrees.

short_def: Two or more motors set up to move together as one.
explanation: Configure it in the Devices menu. Useful for a lift with a motor on each side.
example: Use a motor group for the two lift motors.

short_def: Make a motor turn until told to stop.
explanation: spin keeps going. spin for turns a set amount.
example: Spin the intake forward.

short_def: Spin a motor a set number of degrees or turns, then stop.
explanation: The amount is counted from where the motor is now.
example: Spin the arm motor for 90 degrees.

short_def: Spin a motor to an exact position.
explanation: Good for arms: if 0 is down and 180 is up, the arm goes there from anywhere.
example: Spin the arm to position 180 to lift it.

short_def: How far a motor has turned, in degrees or turns.
explanation: Set it to 0 at a known spot with set position, so the numbers mean something.
example: Reset the arm position to 0 when it's down.

short_def: Unit for counting full turns of a motor. 1 turn = 360 degrees.
example: Spin the spool for 3 turns.

short_def: Twisting force: how hard a motor can turn or lift.
explanation: Lower the max torque to stop a motor breaking a mechanism.
example: Set max torque to 50% so the claw doesn't crush the ball.

short_def: How much electricity a motor is using, in amps.
explanation: High current means the motor is working hard or is stuck.
example: The current is high, so the arm is stuck.

short_def: Push a pneumatic cylinder out, or pull it back in.
explanation: Uses the air stored in the tank. The pump must have filled it first.
example: Extend the cylinder to push the ball out.

short_def: Turn the air pump on to fill the tank, or off to save battery.
explanation: Turn it on at the start so there's air when you need it.
example: Turn the pump on at the start of the match.

short_def: A device that measures something and tells the Brain.
explanation: Code uses sensor values to make decisions, like stopping before a wall.
example: Which sensor can tell the color of the ball?

short_def: Let a sensor measure its starting point before it is used.
explanation: The Inertial Sensor calibrates at the start. Keep the robot still until it finishes.
example: Don't touch the robot while it calibrates.

short_def: Reports True while a button or bumper is being pressed.
explanation: Works for the Bumper Switch, Touch LED, and Brain and controller buttons.
example: Wait until the bumper is pressed.

short_def: Reports True when a sensor detects something in front of it.
explanation: The Distance and Optical Sensors can both do this.
example: If the sensor found an object, close the claw.

short_def: How far away the detected object is, in mm or inches.
example: Drive until the object distance is less than 100 mm.

short_def: A color as a number from 0 to 359, like a spot on a color wheel.
explanation: Red is near 0, green near 120, blue near 240. More exact than color names.
example: The hue is 230, so the ball is blue.

short_def: How much light a sensor sees, from 0% to 100%.
example: Brightness drops when the robot is over the black line.

short_def: Reports True if the sensor sees the chosen color.
example: If the optical sensor detects red, sort the ball left.

short_def: How much charge is left in the battery, as a percent.
example: Print the battery capacity before the match.

short_def: How fast speed is changing. The accelerometer measures it in g.
explanation: 1 g is the pull of gravity. A crash shows up as a big jump.
example: Acceleration jumps when the robot hits the wall.
blocks: (BrainInertial acceleration of [x v] axis in g)

short_def: How a robot tilts or turns: nose up/down, side to side, left/right.
explanation: Measured by the Inertial Sensor. Not the same as pitch for part sizes!
example: The pitch changes when the robot drives up the ramp.

short_def: One picture's worth of data about the objects the vision sensor sees.
explanation: Take a snapshot first, then ask about the objects in it. Take a new one each loop.
example: Take a snapshot, then check if a ball exists.
blocks: get [AI Classifications v] data from [AIVision1 v]

short_def: A type of game object the AI Vision Sensor can recognize by itself.
explanation: It comes pre-trained for the current game's objects.
example: The AI classification says this object is a ball.

short_def: A saved color that the vision sensor looks for.
explanation: Set it up in the Devices menu by showing the sensor the color.
example: We made a color signature for the red cubes.

short_def: A black-and-white square code that the sensor identifies by its ID number.
explanation: Fields can have AprilTags so the robot can work out where it is.
example: The sensor sees AprilTag 3 on the wall.

short_def: How many matching objects are in the snapshot.
example: If the object count is more than 0, drive to the ball.

short_def: Where the object's center is, left to right, in the camera picture.
explanation: The picture is 320 pixels wide, so 160 is the middle. Use it to turn toward an object.
example: centerX is 60, so the ball is to the left.

short_def: One direction of joystick movement, named A, B, C or D.
explanation: Position goes from -100 to 100; 0 is the middle.
example: Axis A controls driving forward and back.

short_def: A button on the controller, like L▲, R▼, E▲ or F▼.
explanation: Each button has a name, so code can check which one is pressed.
example: Press R▲ to raise the arm.

short_def: Show text or numbers on the Brain screen or in the Console.
explanation: Printing sensor values is one of the best ways to find bugs.
example: Print the distance so we can see what the sensor reads.

short_def: Window in VEXcode that shows printed text while a project runs.
explanation: The robot must be connected to the computer.
example: Check the Console to see the values.

short_def: Where the next printed text will appear on the screen.
explanation: Rows go down, columns go across.
example: Set the cursor to row 2 before printing.
blocks: set cursor to next row on screen

short_def: Erase everything on the Brain screen.
example: Clear the screen before printing new values.

short_def: Something that happens, which can start code running.
explanation: Starting the project, pressing a button or receiving a broadcast are all events.
example: Pressing the bumper is an event.

short_def: Hat block that runs its stack when the project starts.
explanation: Every Blocks project needs at least one.
example: Put the drive blocks under when started.

short_def: Send a message that starts every when I receive block with that name.
explanation: Lets one part of a project start another part.
example: Broadcast "score" when the ball is in.

short_def: Hat block that runs when its message is broadcast.
example: When I receive "score", flash the Touch LED green.

short_def: Pause for a number of seconds before the next block.
example: Wait 1 second, then lower the arm.

short_def: Pause until a condition becomes True.
example: Wait until the bumper is pressed.

short_def: Code that repeats.
explanation: repeat, forever, repeat until and while are all loops.
example: Use a loop instead of copying the same blocks 4 times.
blocks:
repeat (4)
drive [forward v] for (300) [mm v] ▶
turn [right v] for (90) degrees ▶
end

short_def: Loop that runs the blocks inside a set number of times.
example: Repeat 4 times: drive 300 mm and turn 90 degrees.

short_def: Loop that keeps running the blocks inside until the project stops.
explanation: Used for driver control and for checking sensors all the time.
example: Put the sensor check in a forever loop.

short_def: Loop that repeats until a condition becomes True.
example: Repeat until the distance is less than 100 mm.

short_def: Loop that repeats as long as a condition is True.
explanation: The opposite check to repeat until.
example: While the button is pressed, spin the intake.

short_def: Run the blocks inside only if the condition is True.
example: If the bumper is pressed, stop driving.

short_def: Run one set of blocks if a condition is True, and another set if not.
example: If the ball is red, go left; else go right.
blocks:
if <[Bumper1 v] pressed?> then
stop driving
else
drive [forward v]
end

short_def: A question with a True or False answer that decides what code runs.
explanation: For example: is the bumper pressed? It goes in the pointed space of if, wait until and repeat until.
example: The condition is: is the distance less than 100?
blocks:
if <([Distance1 v] object distance in [mm v]) < (100)> then
stop driving
end

short_def: Leave a loop right away.
explanation: The project continues with the blocks after the loop.
example: Break out of the loop when the timer reaches 10.

short_def: End the project right away.
example: Stop the project when all the balls are scored.

short_def: Counts seconds since the project started or the timer was reset.
explanation: Useful for stopping an action after a set time.
example: If the timer is over 50 seconds, park the robot.

short_def: Block that does math or compares values.
explanation: +, -, *, /, >, <, =, and, or, not are all operators.
example: Use an operator to add 1 to the score.

aka: greater than; less than; equal to
short_def: Check if a value is greater than, less than or equal to another.
explanation: Reports True or False, so it can be used as a condition.
example: Is the distance less than 100?

short_def: Combine conditions: both true (and), either true (or), the opposite (not).
example: If the ball is red and the claw is open, pick it up.

short_def: Pick a random number between two values.
example: Pick random 1 to 3 to choose a path.

short_def: Change a number to fewer decimal places.
explanation: 3.14159 rounded to 1 decimal place is 3.1.
example: Round the distance before printing it.

short_def: A named box that stores a value your code can read and change.
explanation: For example, a variable called score that counts game pieces.
example: Make a variable called score and set it to 0.

short_def: Add an amount to a variable.
explanation: Use a negative number to subtract.
example: Change score by 1 each time a ball goes in.

short_def: A value that is either True or False.
explanation: Named after the mathematician George Boole.
example: Make a Boolean called hasBall.

short_def: The two possible Boolean values.
example: The bumper pressed block reports True.

short_def: A variable that holds many values in order.
explanation: Each item has a number (index). Blocks start counting at 1, but Python starts at 0!
example: Store the three target distances in a list.

short_def: Your own block, made from other blocks, that you can use again.
explanation: Define it once, then use it anywhere. It keeps long projects tidy.
example: Make a My Block called driveSquare.

short_def: A named set of instructions you can run again by calling its name.
explanation: My Blocks are functions in Blocks. In Python you write them with def.
example: Call the score function after each ball.
blocks:
define driveSquare
repeat (4)
drive [forward v] for (300) [mm v] ▶
turn [right v] for (90) degrees ▶
end

short_def: A value you give a block or function to change what it does.
explanation: In drive for 200 mm, 200 and mm are parameters.
example: Give the function a distance parameter.
blocks:
define drive (distance)
drive [forward v] for (distance) [mm v] ▶

short_def: A typed programming language that VEXcode IQ also supports.
explanation: Python uses the same commands as Blocks, but you type them.
example: Next term we'll start using Python.

short_def: Spaces at the start of a line that show which code is inside a loop or if.
explanation: Python uses indentation instead of C-shaped blocks; use 4 spaces (shown here as ····). Wrong indentation causes errors.
example: Indent the drive command so it's inside the loop.

short_def: The : at the end of a line that starts a loop, if or function.
explanation: Forgetting it is the most common Python error.
example: You forgot the colon after while True.

short_def: Python keyword that creates a function.
example: Use def to make a function called drive_square.

short_def: Load extra code (a library) into a Python program.
explanation: VEXcode adds from vex import * for you at the top.
example: Import random to pick random numbers.

short_def: Text data, written inside quotes.
explanation: "hello" is a string; 5 is a number. Convert a number to a string to join it with text.
example: Print the string "Ready!".

short_def: Whole numbers (integer) and numbers with a decimal point (float).
explanation: 3 is an integer; 3.5 is a float.
example: Distance is a float because it has decimals.

short_def: Instructions that run one after another, in order.
explanation: Order matters: turning then driving ends up somewhere different from driving then turning.
example: Check the sequence: we turn before we drive.
blocks:
drive [forward v] for (300) [mm v] ▶
turn [right v] for (90) degrees ▶
drive [forward v] for (200) [mm v] ▶

short_def: A step-by-step plan for solving a problem.
explanation: Write the algorithm in words before you code it.
example: Our algorithm: find the ball, drive to it, grab it.

short_def: A plan for code written in plain language, not a real programming language.
example: Write pseudocode before building the blocks.

short_def: A mistake in code that makes the robot do the wrong thing.
example: There's a bug: the robot turns the wrong way.

short_def: Find and fix bugs.
explanation: Print values, test one part at a time, and change one thing at a time.
example: Let's debug the turn by printing the heading.
blocks: print ([Distance1 v] object distance in [mm v]) on screen ▶

short_def: A mistake that stops code from running, often a typo.
explanation: Read the error message; it tells you which line to check.
example: The error says line 12 is missing a colon.

short_def: The motors, wheels and frame that move the robot around.
explanation: One of the first design choices. Think about obstacles, speed vs pushing power, and how many motors are left for other jobs. This is the mechanism; the Drivetrain device you set up in VEXcode is CODE-013.
example: We need a drivetrain that can climb over the bar.

short_def: The robot's base frame that everything else is built on.
explanation: The drivetrain is part of the chassis. Towers for arms and lifts are attached to it.
example: Mount the tower in the middle of the chassis.

short_def: Wheels on two sides; it turns by changing each side's speed.
explanation: The most common drivetrain. Can have two motors or more (four-wheel drive, six-wheel drive). It cannot move sideways.
example: Our standard drive has two motors and four wheels.

short_def: Standard drive plus a sideways middle wheel, so it can also slide sideways.
explanation: Four omni wheels plus a fifth omni wheel set sideways between them, with 3 or 5 motors. The middle wheel can get caught on obstacles.
example: With an H drive we can slide sideways into the goal.

short_def: Drivetrain with angled omni wheels that can move in any direction.
explanation: Three or four omni wheels, each with its own motor. Kiwi drive and X drive are holonomic drives. Needs more advanced code than a standard drive.
example: A holonomic drive can strafe without turning.

short_def: Holonomic drive with three omni wheels set 120° apart.
explanation: Uses three motors. Less stable than a four-wheel holonomic drive.

short_def: Holonomic drive with four omni wheels angled at the corners.
explanation: Each wheel has its own motor, so it uses four motors.

short_def: Drivetrain that uses tank treads instead of wheels.
explanation: Very good at driving over obstacles; add Traction Links for more grip. It cannot move sideways.
example: A track drive could climb onto the platform.

short_def: Able to move in any direction, including sideways, without turning.
explanation: H drives and holonomic drives are omni-directional; standard and track drives are not. Omni wheels (BLD-049) make it possible.
example: Is it worth building an omni-directional robot for this game?

short_def: The area between where the robot's outer wheels touch the ground.
explanation: A bigger footprint makes the robot more stable and less likely to tip, especially when an arm or lift is raised.
example: Make the footprint wider so it doesn't tip when the arm is up.

short_def: The height from the ground to the lowest part of the robot.
explanation: More ground clearance makes it easier to drive over obstacles. Bigger wheels give more ground clearance.
example: We need more ground clearance to get over the pipe.

short_def: A mechanism that moves or handles objects to do a task.
explanation: Arms, claws, intakes and plows are manipulators. Design it for the object (size, shape, weight) and for how it must move it (push, pull, lift).
example: Our manipulator needs to pick up two pins at once.

short_def: A manipulator with no motor, like a plow.
explanation: It is moved by the drivetrain or another mechanism, sometimes with rubber band energy. Quick to build, and it saves motors for other jobs.
example: A passive manipulator saves us a motor.

short_def: A manipulator powered by a motor, like an arm, claw or intake.
explanation: It can be controlled with code or the Controller. Takes more time and planning to build than a passive manipulator.

short_def: Passive manipulator on the drivetrain for pushing game pieces.
explanation: Also stops the robot driving up onto game pieces and getting stuck.
example: Add a plow so we can push the cubes into the zone.

short_def: Passive prongs that slide under a game piece to pick it up.
explanation: A kind of passive claw, usually on the end of an arm.

short_def: Passive part that catches onto a game piece or a bar.
explanation: A kind of passive claw. A hook on an arm can let the robot lift itself off the ground.

short_def: Passive wall that keeps game pieces from getting into the robot.
Ramp that lets game pieces slide out into a goal or scoring zone.
Container on the robot that holds several game pieces.
Active manipulator that pulls objects into the robot.
explanation: A motor spins rollers, wheels, belts or flaps that grab the object. Reverse the motor to push it back out (outtake). Design it for the object's shape and weight and how many you want to hold.
example: Our intake can hold two balls.

short_def: Push objects back out of an intake by running it in reverse.
example: Outtake the ball into the goal.

short_def: Moving belt or chain that carries game pieces through the robot.
explanation: Often built from chain or tank tread with Intake Flaps.

short_def: Gripper that opens and closes to pick up and carry objects.
explanation: Usually on the end of an arm, moved by a motor through gears or sprockets. Rubber bands, Intake Flaps or Traction Links add grip. Design it for the object's size, shape and weight.
example: The claw keeps dropping the cube, so let's add more grip.

short_def: Claw with one moving side that clamps against a fixed side.
Claw where both sides move, like on the Clawbot.
explanation: Usually two meshing gears move the two sides in opposite directions.

short_def: Claw with spinning rollers that pull objects in and push them out.
explanation: Built from wheels, intake belts or tank tread. Needs less lining up than other claws, but takes more time to build.

short_def: A mechanism that moves like a human arm to lift and move objects.
explanation: Usually attached to a tower on the chassis and moved by a motor through gears or sprockets. Rubber bands can help it lift. Arms move in an arc; lifts move straight up.
example: The arm is too slow; try a different gear ratio.

short_def: Upright structure on the chassis that holds an arm's pivot.
example: Brace the tower so the arm doesn't wobble.

short_def: A single arm that pivots, so its end moves in an arc.
explanation: The easiest arm to build, but what it carries tilts as it lifts.

short_def: Arm made of pivoting bars, often a parallelogram, that stays level.
explanation: Keeps what it carries mostly level as it lifts. 4-bar, 6-bar, chain-bar and double reverse 4-bar are linkage arms.

short_def: Linkage arm with two parallel bars, so the end stays mostly level.
explanation: The Clawbot (2nd gen) uses one. It still moves in a slight arc.
example: A 4-bar keeps the claw level.

short_def: Two 4-bars linked together so the arm reaches higher.
explanation: Reaches higher than a 4-bar but sticks out further as it lifts, so the robot may tip. Usually needs two motors.

short_def: Arm that uses sprockets and chain, not a second bar, to stay level.
explanation: No bars collide, so it can lift high, but if the chain breaks the arm fails.

short_def: Two 4-bars geared together to lift high and nearly straight up.
explanation: The highest reach and straightest lift of the arms, but it needs the most planning. Built in pairs. Careful: the robot can tip with it raised.

short_def: Mechanism that raises things straight up, or lifts the robot.
explanation: Usually driven by gears or sprockets, sometimes helped by rubber bands. An arm moves in an arc; a lift moves vertically.

short_def: Lift where a carriage slides along a track, driven by a rack gear.
explanation: VEX IQ linear motion parts (BLD-065, BLD-066, BLD-075) can be used to build one.

short_def: Lift with stages that slide up each other, pulled by chain.
explanation: Built in pairs. Each extra stage reaches higher.

short_def: Lift of crossed bars that open like scissors to push up.
explanation: Can reach high, but it is one of the hardest mechanisms to build and keep stable.

short_def: Arm that is pulled back, then released to throw an object.
explanation: VEX IQ catapults are usually powered by rubber bands; a motor pulls the arm down to load it. The Hero Bots Fling and Swish use catapults.
example: Tune the catapult with one more rubber band.

short_def: Launcher that shoots objects with a fast-spinning wheel.
explanation: The object is fed into the spinning wheel. A heavier flywheel (BLD-028) stores more energy, so its speed drops less after each shot. Balloon tires work well.

short_def: Two or more gears meshed together to pass on turning.
explanation: Meshing gears turn in opposite directions. A gear train can change speed and torque.
example: Add a gear train so the motor can lift the arm.

short_def: The gear turned by the motor, which drives the other gears.
explanation: Also called the input. The same idea applies to sprockets.
example: Put the 12T driving gear on the motor shaft.

short_def: The gear turned by another gear; it moves the wheel or arm.
explanation: Also called the output.

short_def: Driven teeth ÷ driving teeth. It trades speed for torque or back.
explanation: Can be done with gears or with sprockets. Small driving big (12T → 36T = 3:1): 3× torque, 1/3 speed. Big driving small: more speed, less torque.
example: A 3:1 gear ratio gives the arm three times the torque.

short_def: How much a mechanism multiplies force: output force ÷ input force.
explanation: Gear trains change mechanical advantage. More torque always means less speed.

short_def: Two or more gear ratios in a row, multiplied together.
explanation: The middle gears share a shaft. Fling's catapult uses 3:1 then 5:1, which makes 15:1.

short_def: Gear between the driving and driven gears; it doesn't change the ratio.
explanation: Only the first and last gears set the gear ratio. An idler fills a gap or changes direction.

short_def: Moving a motor's power to another shaft, same speed and torque.
explanation: Uses same-size gears or sprockets (a 1:1 ratio), for example to drive a second wheel. With gears, use an odd number between two wheels so they turn the same way.

short_def: The motor turns the wheel or mechanism's shaft itself, with no gears.
explanation: Simple and reliable; you get the motor's own speed and torque. Swish has a direct drive drivetrain.

short_def: A place where moving parts can catch fingers, wires or clothing.
explanation: Gears, chain and wheels are pinch points. Turn them slowly by hand before powering up the robot.
example: Watch the pinch point where the chain meets the sprocket.

short_def: A push or a pull that can change how something moves.
explanation: A robot moves when its force is unbalanced: motor → shaft → wheel → floor.

short_def: Forces that don't cancel out, so the object's motion changes.
explanation: Balanced forces cancel and nothing changes. Unbalanced forces speed an object up, slow it down or change its direction.
example: The robot wins the tug of war when its force is unbalanced.

short_def: The force from a wheel pushing on the floor that moves the robot.
explanation: More traction: the robot pushes harder and climbs better, but turns less easily.
example: Balloon tires have more traction than omni wheels.

short_def: A force that resists when two surfaces rub or slide.
explanation: Friction gives wheels their traction, but also wastes power in shafts and gears.
example: Too much friction in the shaft makes the motor work harder.

short_def: The amount of matter in an object.
explanation: Mass and weight are not the same thing. Every part adds to the robot's mass.

short_def: The balance point of an object, where its mass is centered.
explanation: Mass over the drive wheels gives more traction. Mass to one side makes the robot veer; too high or too far forward and it tips. 重心 is also used.
example: Keep the center of mass low so the robot doesn't tip.

short_def: Driving the robot with the Controller.
explanation: Use the Brain's built-in Drive program or your own code.

short_def: Robot movement controlled entirely by code, with no driver.
explanation: Once it starts, no one can help, so plan carefully, test in stages and set up the same way every time.
example: Our autonomous scores two goals.

short_def: Where the robot starts, and which way it faces, for an autonomous run.
explanation: Mark it on the field and place the robot the same way every time, or the whole run will be off.
example: Line up the starting position with the third hole.

short_def: Breaking a task into small drive and turn steps before coding.
explanation: Better than guess and check: easier to code, to fix, and to agree on as a team.
example: Let's do path planning before we write the code.

short_def: Turn in place: the two sides drive in opposite directions.
Turn where one side drives and the other side stays still.
explanation: Helpful for lining up with a game piece.

short_def: Turn while driving: one side goes faster than the other.
explanation: A shorter path around obstacles.

short_def: Driving style: each joystick controls one side of the drivetrain.
explanation: One of the four Controller drive modes in VEXcode IQ. People sometimes also say "tank drive" for a standard drive.

aka: Left Arcade; Right Arcade; Split Arcade
short_def: Driving style: one joystick axis drives, another turns.
explanation: VEXcode IQ has Left Arcade and Right Arcade (one stick does everything) and Split Arcade (left stick drives, right stick turns).

short_def: Full power until the target is reached, then stop.
explanation: The simplest control. Easy to code, but the robot overshoots and wiggles. PID is smoother.

short_def: Control that slows down smoothly as the robot nears its target.
explanation: P (proportional) reacts to the error now, I (integral) to error that builds up over time, D (derivative) to how fast the error is changing. Each is multiplied by a constant you tune. The IQ Smart Motor already runs PID inside.

short_def: Power set in proportion to the error: far away = fast, close = slow.
explanation: The P in PID, and a good first step: power = kP × error.

short_def: The value a control loop is trying to reach, like 500 mm or 90°.
How far from the target the robot still is: setpoint minus current value.
explanation: Not the same as an error in code (CODE-106).

short_def: Tracking the robot's position and heading on the field with sensors.
explanation: Uses wheel rotation and heading to update the x, y position many times a second. Mostly used by advanced (often V5) teams.

short_def: Steps engineers follow to solve a problem and design a solution.
A limit the design must meet, like size, number of motors or rules.
explanation: Many come from the game manual. List your goals and constraints before you build.
example: One constraint is that we can only use six motors.

short_def: Come up with many ideas quickly, before choosing one.
An early version built to test an idea.
explanation: Build several prototypes, test them, then choose the best one.
example: Let's build a prototype claw first.

short_def: Improve a design by testing, changing and testing again.
example: We iterated on the intake three times.

short_def: A choice based on measured results, not opinions.
explanation: For example, choose the driver by who did best in practice. It keeps hurt feelings out of the decision.

short_def: Researching other teams for ideas for your design and strategy.
explanation: Ask good questions and write down which team you scouted so you can credit them. Scouting is for inspiration, not copying.

short_def: Your team's plan for how the robot will play the game.
explanation: Start robot design from your strategy: how is the robot going to play the game?
example: Our strategy is to score the easy goals first.

short_def: VEX's starting-point robot design for each season's game.
explanation: Build it to learn the game, then test and improve it. Past Hero Bots include Fling, Swish and Huey.

short_def: Where a team records its ideas, decisions, tests and improvements.
explanation: It shows how the team got there, not just what they built. A simple entry: goal, work, evidence, decision, next step. Judges read it.
example: Write today's test results in the engineering notebook.

short_def: A scoring guide that shows what judges look for.
explanation: Use the Engineering Notebook rubric to check your own notebook before an event.

short_def: A short talk where judges ask your team about your robot and work.
explanation: Two or more judges, about 5–10 minutes, at your pit.

short_def: Your team's work area at an event, for repairs between matches.
explanation: Labeled with your team number. Judges come to your pit for interviews.
example: Bring spare batteries to the pit.

short_def: Check that the robot follows the rules before it can play matches.
explanation: Volunteers check size, parts and software against the game manual.

short_def: List of each match's time, field and alliance partner.
Where teams wait just before their match.
explanation: Arrive early with your alliance partner.

short_def: The team member who drives the robot in a match.
explanation: In a Teamwork Challenge match each team has two drivers, who hand off the controller mid-match.

short_def: The adult who supports the team; not at the field during matches.
explanation: Students play the match and speak for themselves.

short_def: Official who scores matches and enforces the rules.
explanation: If you have a question about the score, the drivers ask the referee calmly after the match.

short_def: Volunteer who reviews notebooks and interviews teams for awards.
Match where two teams work together as an alliance to score.
explanation: Cooperative, not against each other. A match lasts 60 seconds.

short_def: The other team you play with in a Teamwork Challenge match.
explanation: Partners are paired randomly. Find your partner before the match to plan a strategy.

short_def: An object robots score with, like a ball, cube or pin.
The official rules for this season's game.
explanation: Includes robot rules (like size and motor limits), scoring and inspection.
example: Check the game manual before we change the robot.

short_def: Plate showing the team number, mounted on the robot.
explanation: The game manual requires the team number on at least two plates, on opposite sides of the robot.
